analysis.one_liner: Moves housing toward permanently affordable, resident-controlled social ownership through direct federal grants, tenant protections, and rent limits.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Banking Committee on February 27, 1989, sent to its housing subcommittee on March 15, and never received a hearing, vote, or further action before the 101st Congress ended in January 1991.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill proposed the largest peacetime restructuring of American housing ever put on paper. It would have required states and cities to adopt tenant protections, eviction limits, and rent controls; prohibited the demolition or sale of subsidized housing to private owners; and committed the federal government to building 200,000 new and rehabilitating 400,000 housing units a year through direct grants to governments, nonprofits, and resident-owned cooperatives rather than through private lenders. Over time, private rental housing could be bought up and converted into permanently non-speculative 'social ownership,' with a financing floor pegged to the size of the mortgage-interest tax break that mostly benefits affluent homeowners.
analysis.who_benefits: Low- and moderate-income renters and homeowners. Tenants would gain just-cause eviction rules, habitability standards, rent controls in areas with housing emergencies, and collective bargaining rights with landlords. Homeowners facing foreclosure could deed their homes to a social entity in exchange for lifetime tenure at an affordable cost. Tenants of subsidized housing would gain due-process eviction protections, resident councils, and a right of first refusal when their building is sold. New residents could buy converted homes at nominal prices with limited-equity resale rules, making homeownership affordable without speculative gains.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Low- and moderate-income renters and homeowners

how_it_helps.text: Requires every state and local government, as a condition of federal housing and infrastructure funds, to adopt anti-discrimination rules, habitability warranties, just-cause eviction protections, and rent, condominium-conversion, and demolition controls wherever a housing emergency exists.

Directs HUD to fund construction of 200,000 new social housing units and rehabilitation of 400,000 units annually in the transition period, financed by direct federal grants rather than private mortgage debt, with $33 billion a year authorized for production and operating subsidies.

Gives low- and moderate-income homeowners facing foreclosure a way to deed their home to a social entity in exchange for lifetime security of tenure at a monthly cost based on ability to pay, and lets elderly homeowners trade their home for an equity-based annuity.

Prohibits the displacement of low- and moderate-income tenants from federally assisted housing, bans demolition of public and subsidized housing without one-for-one replacement, and blocks conversion of subsidized units to private ownership, including a moratorium on prepayment of subsidized mortgages.
Lets tenants of subsidized buildings exercise a right of first option to buy their projects at federally capped prices, with rehabilitation and operating subsidies attached.

analysis.who_pays: Private landlords, real estate investors, and mortgage lenders, whose rental properties would become subject to rent caps, tenant bargaining rights, and a standing local-government offer to buy them out for conversion to social ownership. Taxpayers would fund the authorizations — roughly $56 billion a year across the bill's titles, with a floor tied to the annual cost of federal homeowner tax deductions — and state and local governments would bear new mandates enforced by withholding federal highway, sewer, and development funds.

drawbacks.text: The bill authorizes roughly $56 billion a year across its titles and sets a minimum annual authorization equal to the federal tax expenditures for mortgage interest and property tax deductibility, and even allows the required funds to be drawn from national security accounts if not otherwise appropriated — an enormous, open-ended federal commitment.

It overrides local control: every state and city must adopt federally prescribed rent, eviction, and conversion ordinances or lose federal money not just for housing but for highways, sewers, and economic development, with courts empowered to block funding for noncompliant plans.

After fiscal 1991, no federal money could be spent on building or rehabilitating any housing other than social housing or housing converting to it, eliminating federal support for private construction entirely.

Mandated rent caps and conversion prohibitions, and a standing government offer to buy rental properties, could reduce incentives to build and maintain rental housing outside the social sector, and the government purchases themselves would depend on appropriations Congress might never make at the authorized levels.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For renters and owners of modest means, the promised benefits were sweeping: permanent affordability, security of tenure, and an alternative to relying on private landlords and mortgage markets. But the costs and risks were equally sweeping — an annual price tag on the scale of the entire existing housing budget, a unprecedented federal mandate dictating local landlord-tenant law under threat of cutting off highway and sewer money, and a phase-out of federal support for all privately developed housing. Even sympathetic housing-policy observers would question whether the financing and the federal-state machinery as drafted could have worked; the bill read more as a full alternative housing system than a workable statute.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Banking Committee and its housing subcommittee for the rest of the 101st Congress and died there when the Congress ended in January 1991.

narrative.text: Rep. Ronald Dellums of California introduced the National Comprehensive Housing Act on February 27, 1989; it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Banking, Finance and Urban Affairs.
Seven House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republican did, and the sponsors amounted to 7 of the 257 House Democrats.
On March 15, 1989, the bill was referred to the Subcommittee on Housing and Community Development — the last action ever taken on it.
No hearings, markup, committee vote, or floor action followed, and the bill died when the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private landlords, real estate investors, and mortgage lenders kept the existing housing system untouched: no rent controls, no conversion of rental stock to social ownership, and no prohibition on selling subsidized housing to private owners. Taxpayers avoided the roughly $56-billion-a-year commitment. Low- and moderate-income tenants and homeowners gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Landlords, lenders, and real estate investors

for.name: Rep. Ronald V. Dellums
for.what_they_did: Introduced the National Comprehensive Housing Act and assembled the bill's program of tenant protections, rent controls, and federally funded social housing.

for.name: 7 of 257 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican signed on.

against.name: House Committee on Banking, Finance and Urban Affairs
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never reported it out; no markup or vote was held.

against.name: Subcommittee on Housing and Community Development
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on March 15, 1989 and took no further action on the bill for the remainder of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never advanced far enough for a vote; all eight sponsors were Democrats and no Republican cosponsored, but the chamber as a whole never weighed in.

industries.industry: Private landlords and rental property owners
industries.note: Rent controls, just-cause eviction, mandatory tenant bargaining, and a permanent government offer to purchase their buildings would have capped returns and funneled rental properties into nonprofit or public ownership. The bill's defeat left their business model intact.

industries.industry: Mortgage lenders and real estate finance
industries.note: The bill aimed to replace privately controlled mortgage debt and equity capital with direct federal grants for housing production, and it would have placed foreclosed and fully-paid rental properties with local governments instead of lenders and investors. Its failure preserved the private mortgage-and-development financing system.

Conversion of rental buildings to condominiums would have been prohibited in housing-emergency areas except with supermajority tenant approval or conversion to social ownership. The prohibition never took effect.

Direct grants for 200,000 new and 400,000 rehabilitated units a year would have been a massive source of construction work, with Davis-Bacon prevailing wages and a preference for union shops and worker-owned suppliers — but development priority went to nonprofits, cooperatives, and public agencies over for-profit builders, and after 1991 only social housing could receive federal construction money.

The bill banned converting subsidized units to private ownership, imposed a moratorium on mortgage prepayments, and threatened noncompliant owners with regulatory foreclosure and resale to tenants or social owners. None of these restrictions was enacted.
